title: Root Canal Aftercare: What to Do in the First 48 Hours
metaTitle: Root Canal Aftercare: The First 48 Hours
metaDescription: A practical guide to root canal aftercare in the first 48 hours — eating, managing soreness, protecting the temporary filling, and when to call a dentist.
secondaryKeywords: caring for tooth after root canal
excerpt: What to do in the two days after a root canal: when to eat, how to ease soreness, and how to protect the treated tooth.
heroImageAlt: A person holding a glass of water and a soft meal at a kitchen table after a dental appointment.
bodyHtml:
In the first 48 hours after a root canal, the goals are simple: wait until the numbness fully wears off before eating, chew on the opposite side of your mouth, keep the area clean, and manage any soreness with over-the-counter pain relief if your dentist agrees. Most people feel steadily better within a day or two, and these early habits help the tooth settle while you wait for the final restoration.

The first few hours

Your mouth will likely stay frozen for one to three hours after treatment. During that window, it is easy to accidentally bite your cheek, lip, or tongue without feeling it, so it is best to hold off on eating until sensation returns. Warm (not hot) drinks are usually fine. If you were given specific instructions by your dental team, follow those first, since they are based on what was actually done to your tooth.

Managing soreness

Some tenderness around the tooth and jaw is normal, especially when a tooth was already inflamed or infected before treatment. The soreness is often most noticeable for the first two to three days and then eases. Many people find an over-the-counter pain reliever helpful, but you should confirm what is appropriate for you, particularly if you take other medications or have health conditions. A cold compress on the cheek for short periods can also reduce discomfort. If pain is severe, worsening, or not responding to anything, that is a reason to contact your dentist rather than wait it out.

Eating and drinking

Once the freezing is gone, stick to softer foods for the first day or two and chew on the side away from the treated tooth. A tooth that still has only a temporary filling is more vulnerable, and hard or sticky foods can loosen it or stress the tooth. Think yogurt, eggs, pasta, soup that has cooled, mashed vegetables, and similar easy options. You can usually return to a more normal diet as the tooth feels comfortable, but avoid heavy chewing on that side until your permanent restoration is in place.

Keeping the area clean

Continue brushing and flossing, including gently around the treated tooth. Good hygiene supports healing and does not disturb the work that was done. If your gums are a little tender, brush softly in that spot rather than skipping it. A warm salt-water rinse a couple of times a day can feel soothing, but it is a comfort measure, not a substitute for the permanent restoration your tooth still needs.

Protecting the temporary filling

Many root canals finish with a temporary filling that seals the tooth until a crown or permanent filling is placed. Treat it carefully: avoid chewing gum, hard candy, nuts, and sticky foods on that side. If a temporary filling comes out or feels noticeably different, call your dental office for advice. Leaving a tooth unsealed for a long time can allow bacteria back in, which is one reason follow-up appointments matter.

Is it normal for the tooth to feel different when I bite?

A mild, dull tenderness when biting is common in the early days. However, if the tooth feels clearly "high" or hits before your other teeth, mention it to your dentist, as the bite may need a small adjustment.

Can I go to work or school the next day?

Most people return to their usual routine the same day or the next day, since a standard root canal uses local anaesthetic rather than sedation. How you feel is individual, so give yourself a quieter day if you need one.

When should I call the dentist?

Reach out if you have swelling that is spreading, a fever, pain that keeps getting worse after the first couple of days, an allergic reaction, or a lost temporary filling. Timely follow-up is part of a good outcome.

Planning your next step

A root canal is usually only part of the journey; the tooth still needs its final restoration to protect it long term.
